title: The King Who Ordered the Army for Rāma
tease: A reciter says Rāma is outnumbered in battle. King Kulaśēkhara does not wait for the next verse—he orders his own army to help.

source.work: Śrīvaiṣṇava Guruparamparā traditions; Kulaśēkhara Āḻvār, Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi
source.locus: Kulaśēkhara Āḻvār caritam — Rāmāyaṇa recitation and army-order episode; compare the Rāma-centred decads of Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi as the earlier poetic witness
source.traditionNote: The episode in which Kulaśēkhara orders real troops to help Rāma belongs to later Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography. His own Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi is the earlier textual witness to his intense imaginative identification with Rāma's world; it does not narrate the army-order scene as autobiography.

variants.differs: Later retellings expand the core episode differently: some emphasize the Khara battle, some summarize repeated attempts to intervene, and some turn the image into a march toward Laṅkā.
variants.tellings: The stable hagiographic core is that a Rāmāyaṇa recitation makes Rāma's danger so immediate to the king that he orders his own forces to help, and the reciter advances to Rāma's victory to calm the command.
variants.weTell: We use the Khara-battle army-order form and disclose the broader Laṅkā/repeated-intervention versions as later retelling variants.

sourcing.claim: Later Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography remembers Kulaśēkhara as a king intensely absorbed in hearing the Rāmāyaṇa recited.
During the recitation of Rāma's battle with Khara and a large rākṣasa force, Kulaśēkhara hears Rāma as being in present danger.
The king orders his own army to prepare to assist Rāma.
The reciter advances to Rāma's victory so the king understands that no intervention is needed and the order can stop.

blocks.text: Later Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography remembers King «Kulaśēkhara Āḻvār» as a listener who could not keep the Rāmāyaṇa safely inside a story.
One day a reciter reached the battle in which «Rāma» stands against Khara and a vast army of rākṣasas. The king heard that Rāma was facing the enemy with only a few companions.
For Kulaśēkhara, listening was no longer enough.
He ordered his own troops to prepare. If Rāma was in danger, a king with soldiers had no business sitting in a hall while the battle went on without him.
Courtiers and the reciter had a practical problem: the battle belonged to an ancient epic, not to a road they could march down that afternoon.
The reciter solved it by continuing quickly to the part where Rāma defeats the enemy. Once Kulaśēkhara heard that Rāma had already won, the order to march could stop.
The later saint-life tells the episode to show the king's total absorption in Rāma's story. It is not a claim that his army literally entered the Rāmāyaṇa.
His own Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi gives an earlier poetic witness to that intensity. Across its Rāma poems, Kulaśēkhara speaks from inside the grief, love and longing of the epic's characters.
That is the source boundary Sandhya Katha keeps: the poems show us the voice; the army-march scene is the later biography's picture of what such listening looked like.
The strange thing is not that he forgot fiction. For him, the story carried a duty into the present.

The hagiography makes that response excessive on purpose. A ruler is supposed to know where his kingdom ends and an old story begins. Kulaśēkhara's devotion erases that distance for a moment completely.
Most listeners ask what happens next. Kulaśēkhara heard that Rāma needed help and asked instead: why are we still sitting here?
Later Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography remembers King «Kulaśēkhara Āḻvār» as a ruler whose love of the Rāmāyaṇa did not stay politely on the other side of the storyteller's voice.

At court, the epic would be recited aloud. For most listeners, the sequence was familiar: exile, forest, danger, battle, return. Kulaśēkhara listened as though the distance between then and now had narrowed.
One episode became famous in the saint-life.
The reciter reached the battle where «Rāma» faces Khara and his rākṣasa forces. The king heard that Rāma was in danger and that the enemy was numerous.
He did not respond like an audience member waiting for the next verse.
He responded like a king who had troops.

Kulaśēkhara ordered the army to prepare. If Rāma needed help, then help should be sent. The fact that the battle belonged to an ancient epic did not, for that moment, reduce the urgency he heard in it.
The court now had a problem the Rāmāyaṇa itself could not solve for them. Their king was ready to move real soldiers toward a battle that had already been sung for generations.
The reciter continued quickly.
He reached the part where Rāma defeats the enemy. Once Kulaśēkhara heard that the danger had passed and Rāma had won, the military order could be withdrawn.
Later biographies sometimes expand the image into repeated moments of the king wanting to intervene in Rāma's story, and modern retellings sometimes turn that into a march toward Laṅkā.

Sandhya Katha keeps the stable core narrower: the saint-life remembers a king so absorbed in the Rāmāyaṇa that a narrated danger becomes a present duty, and his court must bring him back by completing the episode.
That hagiographic scene is later than Kulaśēkhara's own poetry.

His Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi is the earlier textual witness. In its Rāma-centred decads, the poet repeatedly speaks from inside the emotional world of the epic: as a mother, a father, a separated lover, or a devotee who does not keep the characters at a comfortable distance.
The poems do not say, I once ordered my army into Rāma's battle.
They show something more fundamental: an imagination that inhabits the story instead of merely observing it.
That difference matters because biography and poetry are doing different work.

The poem lets us hear the devotion in Kulaśēkhara's own literary voice. The later hagiography turns that intensity into a scene everyone can remember: a king interrupts a recitation because he thinks the hero needs reinforcements.
The story is funny, but it is not only a joke about a confused listener.

Kulaśēkhara knows what duty means. Kings are judged by whether they act when protection is needed. The hagiography asks what happens when a story becomes vivid enough to activate that same sense of duty.
For a moment, the answer is absurdly practical: call the troops.
Then the reciter has to use the story itself to release the king from the command. Rāma has won. No army is needed.
The episode also says something about listening.
A distant story can remain entertainment, even when its values are admired. Or it can move close enough to disturb the listener's habits.
Kulaśēkhara's reaction is extreme because saint-lives make extremes memorable. Sandhya Katha does not ask children to confuse stories with current events or act without checking reality.
The useful question is smaller: has a story ever made you feel responsible for something outside yourself?
That is where the old hagiographic joke becomes interesting.
Kulaśēkhara does not only want to know whether Rāma survives.
He wants to know why, if help is needed, he is not already helping.
The army never reaches the ancient battlefield.
The poem and the biography reach us instead.
His own verses preserve the emotional nearness of Rāma's world. The later life-story gives that nearness marching orders.
Most audiences hear danger in a story and lean forward.
Kulaśēkhara heard it and reached for the responsibilities of a king.
The reciter had to finish the battle before the king could sit down again.

close.question: What is the difference between enjoying a story and letting it make you feel responsible for something?
close.seed: A story becomes close when its values start asking something of the listener.

ifTheyAsk.q: Did Kulaśēkhara really try to send soldiers into the Rāmāyaṇa?
ifTheyAsk.a: That is how later Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography tells the episode. Sandhya Katha presents it as saint-life, not as a modern historical report.

Some later retellings broaden the story that way. The form we follow is narrower: during the Khara battle recitation, he orders troops to help Rāma, and the reciter continues to Rāma's victory so the order can stop.

ifTheyAsk.q: Is the army episode in his own poems?
ifTheyAsk.a: No. His Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi is the earlier poetic witness to his intense Rāma devotion. The army-order scene belongs to the later biography.
